title: Full of grace and truth (John 1:6–18)
hook: the Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us

segments.voice: Yesterday, Logos: the Word in the beginning, and a light the darkness can't put out. Your line: the light shines in the darkness.

A tent goes up in a field, right next to yours. Same mud, same rain, same mosquitoes. Somebody has decided to camp where you camp. In the book of Exodus, the people of Israel live in tents in the wilderness, and in the middle of the camp stands a tent for God: the tabernacle, which the glory of the LORD fills. John has said the Word was with God in the beginning. Today he says how the Word came close, and he says it with a tent.

First, a man sent from God named John, the Baptist, who came as a witness to the light. He wasn't the light, John says carefully; he came to point to it. Then the light comes into the world, and the world doesn't know him. He came to his own, and his own didn't receive him. But to as many as did, he gave power to become children of God. Then, in the King James words: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth." Made flesh. Not a costume, not a visit: skin, hunger, tiredness. Christians call this the incarnation, from the Latin for in flesh. And dwelt: the Greek verb literally means pitched a tent. The Word set up camp among us, the way God's presence lived in the tabernacle. Full of grace and truth. Grace is a gift you didn't earn; truth is what's real, even when it's hard. It's easy to find one without the other: kindness that won't be honest, or honesty that isn't kind. John says in this one person they come together. Then: "And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace." The Greek is grace instead of grace, or grace on top of grace, and some modern versions say grace upon grace, like waves arriving on a shore. And the passage ends: no one has ever seen God, but the one close to the Father's heart has made him known.
screen: then, large: `OF HIS FULNESS HAVE ALL WE RECEIVED.`

segments.voice: Think of one person who told you something true and hard, and stayed kind while saying it, a coach, a parent, a friend, a doctor: it stung, and you knew they were on your side. Then picture someone who needs a true word from you, and imagine saying it gently, with no wish to win. If you pray, ask for both.
Skene, the Greek word for a tent, the root of dwelt, pitched his tent: how John describes the Word made flesh, camping among us full of grace and truth.
Your line: grace upon grace. One gift arriving on top of another. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In the Angelus, a traditional Catholic prayer, people bow or kneel at the line 'and the Word was made flesh', and some churches bow in the Creed at the words about the incarnation.

fork.setup: you're John, writing how God came close. you have one verb for how the Word lived among people. which do you choose?
fork.reveal: John's verb, skenoo, means to pitch a tent: "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us", the way God's glory dwelt in the tabernacle.

original.note: Greek: he pitched his tent, he dwelt. from skene, a tent, the word used for the tabernacle.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus came to live on earth.
what it means: God's own Word became flesh, set up camp among people, and was full of grace and truth at once.

what a scholar hears: eskenosen, 'pitched his tent', recalls the tabernacle; 'grace for grace' is charin anti charitos, grace replacing or piled on grace; and 'we beheld his glory' echoes the glory that filled the tabernacle.
recall: from a Persian word for a walled garden
guess: a tent, as in the Word pitched his tent among us
the curtain hiding the holy place in the temple
a shepherd's staff used to guide the flock

chat.says: What does John mean when he says the Word dwelt among us?
options: The Greek says pitched a tent: God's Word camped among people, in real flesh.
That God's Word visited briefly in a vision, then went back up to heaven.
That the Word lived only inside the temple, like the tabernacle before it.
chat.meaning: Dwelt literally means pitched a tent. The Word was made flesh and set up camp among us, the way God's presence lived in the tabernacle.

tabernacle.meaning: the tent for God in the middle of Israel's camp

Exodus.meaning: the Bible book of Israel's journey through the wilderness

incarnation.meaning: from the Latin for in flesh: the Word made flesh

only begotten.meaning: an old phrase for one and only

sources.quoted: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.
And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.

notes: The carry 'grace upon grace' is a modern rendering; the KJV of John 1:16 reads 'grace for grace'. Both appear.
σκηνόω / σκηνή and the tabernacle (Exodus 40:34–35): standard commentary. Confirm.
John 1:18: some important manuscripts read 'only begotten God' (μονογενὴς θεός), others 'only begotten Son'. Mentioned only in the trapdoor. Confirm.
Custom of bowing or kneeling at 'the Word was made flesh' (e.g. at the Angelus, the Last Gospel, the Creed at 'incarnate'). Confirm phrasing in howItsDone.
Teach: 'the passage ends' paraphrases 1:18 (the Father's 'bosom' rendered 'heart').
